Using Transformer-Based Models to Model Cell-Cell Interactions Within the Cancer Tumor Microenvironment
Emmanuel Alawode1
1Department of Computing and Games, Teesside University, Street, Postcode, Middlesbrough, United Kingdom
Abstract

Understanding of cell-cell interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) in cancer research cannot be under stated as these interactions govern the critical processes such as immune evasion, metastasis and tumor progression. With recent advancement in spatial transcriptomics, it is now possible to analyze gene expression at the subcellular while retaining spatial context, bridging the gap between single-cell RNA- sequencing and bulk transccriptomic profiling. This study presents a novel approach to leveraging transformer- based models, specifically adapted to model cell-cell interactions within the TME. The pipeline in this study preprocessed tissue samples through a modular framework that imitates human in the loop approach to clean, cluster and annotate cell states, enabling the extraction of biologically and spatially meaningful features. This includes spatial context, tissue type, cancer scores mitochondrial activity and cell reactivity, among other metrics. To accommodate these features, various components of the base model used in this study were adapted specifically for spatial transcriptomic data. A structured sequencing language was developed and to serve as language tokens which were included into the vocabulary of the model with the help of a custom tokenizer built with a normalization module designed to retain biological tokens in their intended form, ensuring the preservation of biological and spatial semantics within tokenized sequences. To further guide the model in its training process, a tailored masking strategy was implemented to prioritize learning contextually significant embeddings withing the cell state sequence to effectively control the token prediction priority during learning. This helped the model reduce probability of masking fixed reference tokens while emphasizing dynamic and heterogeneous features. The adapted BERT model leverages it bidirectional and positional encoding efficiency to capture spacial and functional dependencies between cells. This study goes further to highlight the transformative potential of leveraging transformer architectures within the field of single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA seq)
Key words: Spatial transcriptomics, Malignancy, Tokenizer, Gene Expression
Introduction

Cells have been proven to communicate with their environment and neighboring cells through various methods. This intricate interplay has been the focal point of numerous studies, particularly in cancer research, where understanding the interactions between cancer cells and their tumor microenvironment (TME) has been pivotal. Cell-to-cell communication is a process by which cells interact and exchange information with each other to coordinate their activities and maintain homeostasis within tissues and organs. This communication is fundamental to the functioning of multicellular organisms, enabling cells to regulate growth, immune responses, tissue repair, and other biological processes in the organism Song et al..

Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics give us the ability to analyze and explore effectively, cells and their gene expressions at the subcellular level while retaining useful spatial context of cells on the tissue by enabling the mapping of gene expression directly to the sections of the tissue to which they belong. This helps bridge the gap between traditional transcriptomic profiling techniques, such as bulk RNA-seq and single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq).

Data pre-processing was split into 7 modules that were interchangeable and expandable but shared the same state with other modules in their pipeline. Each module had it’s own independent arguments that control the modules behavior and could be fine-tuned based on the requirements of the dataset being processed. These modules are dynamic but needed to add derived columns used during feature extraction.

The first module of the pipeline is the initiator which sets the initial state and default values for logging and configuration for plots throughout the pipeline. The second module is the data loader which handles loading of the dataset from the specified directory and performs initial filtering. This module filters out cells with high mitochondrial and ribosomal activity because excessive activity from either genes could be an indication of damaged or dying cells and artificially introduced technical noise such as uneven fixation or sequencing errors. A curated list by the BROAD Institute of ribosomal genes was used to filter identify existing ribosomal genes in the dataset. The third module calculates quality control metrics largely based on a set of pre-processing methods by Scater McCarthy et al. [2017]. Feature extraction

In the field of analyzing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), the AnnData object stands as a rich data structure that holds a lot of information that can be used to infer cell behaviors and attributes for analysis. But not all of the information captured within the structure is useful for training deep learning models. To prepare the data for extraction, 8 major features were distilled from the pre-processed data based on their ability to convey significant information about a cells state. The first feature, tissue type, is pivotal in providing context about the TME of the cell. With tissue-level awareness, the model can better adapt to the variations in gene expression and cellular behaviour that are tied to specific tissue. This is particularly crucial in cancer research where the cellular environment can significantly influence functional and interaction changes. Next, spatial context [x, y] of the cells were added as another feature. The distances were taken from the AnnData and then max-normalized. Max normalization was done by setting the maximum distance to 1 and then scaling down other values to match. This was done to reduce distance value ranges as this simplifies computation and brings the datasets of varying sizes to the same scale while preserving relative relationships between the distances.The cancer cell score that was derived during pre-processing was referenced and added to the feature set. Following the R-implementation of Seurat Satija et al. [2015], gene expression variability was analyzed. This focused on how different genes behaved across the sampled tissue. These highly-variable-genes (HVGs) are genes that are expressed in high variability across the TME as excluding gene variability reduces the efficiency in capturing cell heterogeneity. For each cell a fixed number of highly expressed HVGs were extracted and added to the

feature list. Mitochondrial activity was evaluated by computing the total expression of genes connected with mitochondria. The expression values of mitochondrial genes were tallied, and its sum was compared to the total expression count for the current cell. The expression values were then converted into percentage, with each expression sum an the divisor being multiplied 100. The mitochondrial activity of a cell provides cellular energy metabolism and is a good indicator of cell health.
Cell reactivity

The cell reactivity Sr is a score given to each cell based on it’s tendency to interact with other cells. The reactivity strength of the cells were calculated by extracting the graph adjacency matrix and converting them into a numpy array. Then the pair-wise euclidean distances between all spatial coordinates were calculated resulting in a matrix of distances where each element [i, j] represents the euclidean distance between the spatial coordinates of spot i and j. The inverse of each element on the matrix was calculated and the diagonal of the matrix was filled with infinity to avoid zero-divisions when calculating the inverses. Deriving the inverses converts the distances into a measure of proximity where higher inverse distance depicts closer cell spots which were later summed up to get the reactivity strength of a spot. Separate weights were assigned to the graph adjacency and the spatial distances giving higher weights to the spatial distances to increase spatial influence. The values for connectivities and distances were then brought to the same scale with min-max normalization and summed up to give the final reactivity score.
Si = σ · Gi − min(G) max(G) − min(G) · β · Pi − min(P ) max(P ) − min(P )

where Sr is the reactivity score for cell i, Gi is the graph-based connectivity score, Pi is the spatial score, a and b are weights given to the connectivity scores and distance scores respectively, min(G) and max(G) are the minimum and maximum of G, min(P ) and M ax(P ) are the minimum and maximum of P respectively and σ and β are weights assigned to the connectivities and distances respectively.
Cell-cell interaction score

After getting cell reactivity scores, cell-cell interaction scores for each cell and it’s neighbors were calculated. Connectivities and distances were calculated the same way as they were for reactivity score without deriving the mean. The weights used to derive cell reactivity was applied on the conectivites and spatial distances to ensure spatial context was assigned a slightly higher weight value while aligning with the current cells reactivity score value. Hence one score was assigned to each neighbor of the cell. For each cell, a list of length n of neighbors with the highest interactivity score was added to each cells feature. Each neighbor item had its normalized spatial location added to it as a feature. The distance between the neighboring cell and the current cell was calculated based on the euclidean distance between the spatial coordinates of both cells.

Border cells

In this study, a cluster of cells are referred to as a community and cells that are located at the edges of these communities are referred to as Border Cells. To identify border cells, the cluster composition of each cell’s neighbors was analyzed. A threshold was set as the higher limit of spatially close neighbors belonging a different community a cell has to have, to be considered a border cell. To determine an optimal threshold for higher limit, the sum of every cells neighbors with different communities was compiled into a list, then the nth percentile of the number of neighbors every cell had was used to set a threshold. This is crucial as it takes into consideration the distribution of differing neighbors cross the tissue sample thus, allowing threshold to be adaptable to different tissue sizes.
Tokenization

To perform fine-tuning on the model, training data had to be created from the features that had been extracted. A corpus of well structured sequences was constructed using the extracted features where each sequence holds interpreted feature attributes that convey the state of an individual cell. Every cell sequence within the corpus was structured to have the same sequential arrangement thus, giving equal positional interpretation to every point in the sequence for all sequences with each position holding its own significance in cell state interpretation.Tokens are the smallest unit of text than be processed by Natural Language Processing (NLP) models. Each token could either be a single character or a sequence of characters. Tokens do not hold any inherent meaning on their own and this flexibility allows for them to be used in as representations of any kind of information given that they are reflective of the input data’s structure and content. In BERT- based models, tokens play a pivotal role in encoding text into numerical representations (embeddings). Specific tokens, known as special tokens, can be pre-assigned meanings and included in the tokenizer for specific purposes. For instance default tokens like [CLS] which denotes the start of a sequence and SEP which serves as a separator for different segments within a sequence. In this project, custom special tokens were introduced to enhance the interpretability and functionality of the tokenized sequences. These tokens were strategically designed to denote sequence pointers and mark critical locations within the sequences. BERT relies on the positions of tokens to understand the relationship between the tokens in a sequence. By incorporating custom tokens, the tokenizer was tailored to guide BERTs understanding on the positional embeddings within the sequence. Every position within the sequence held the same meaning with the custom tokens separating the segments of the sequence.

A total of 11 custom special tokens were introduced. The token arrangement for each sequence was designed to encode the extracted features into a structured format that aligns with the requirements of the BERT model. Each sequence begins with a [CLS] token, which serves as a classier token that pools

information from the entire sequence. This is followed by the [TISSUE] token and its associated value T , which encodes the type of the cell belongs to, providing tissue level biological identifier. The [SPATIAL] token introduces the spatial context of the cell, represented by the coordinates x and y, which situate the cell within its tissue environment. Next, the [CANCER] token precedes the cancer score Cs which depicts the degree of malignancy of the cell, contributing to a nuanced understanding of the cells pathological context. The cancer score is followed by a series of gene related tokens where each entity includes the [GENE] token which marks the start of a gene expression entity, followed by the gene-specific attributes GnN , GnE and GnD , which represent the gene name, expression level, and dispersion, relatively. these attributes are computed for the top n highly variable genes (HVGs) expressed within the cell, offering a concise and detailed snapshot of its transcriptional activity. The [IS BORDER] token is a custom special token that provides an indicator of whether the cell is at the border of its community. The border denoting token is followed by a set of tokens that reflect neighborhood information of the cell. Each spot starts with a [NEIGHBOR] token followed by value tokens Nnx, Nny, Nd and Nθ Ni with Nnx and Nny denoting representing the spatial coordinates of the nth neighbor, Nd denoting the euclidean distance to the neighbor, Nθ indicating the angular position, and Ni identifying the neighbors interactivity score. Finally, the MITO MED token encodes information related to the mitochondrial activity within the cell, a potential indicator of cellular energy states or stress responses. The sequence concludes with the [SEP] token as shown in figure 4. Final token sequence is given as [CLS] [TISSUE] T [SPATIAL] x y [CANCER] Cs [GENE] GnN GnE GnD [IS BORDER] [NEIGHBOR] Nnx Nny Nd Nθ Ni [MITO MED] [SEP]

A custom tokenizer was built to accommodate the biological and spatial tokens that have been introduced into the models vocabulary. The special tokens were collated and added into the tokenizer, then gene names were explicitly incorporated into the vocabulary. Each gene is prefixed with a unique identifier ”gene ”, to distinguish it from other text elements and maintain it’s biological relevance. This approach avoids ambiguities that may arise from overlapping meanings with common words, ensuring precise representation of gene-related information. IN every cell sequence, the values are designed to be treated as single tokens, but this is not the default behavor of the default tokenizer. The custom tokenizer was adapted to do this by applying transformations which prepare the sequence for model consumption. These transformations ensure that the characters are tokenized in a way that is both meaningful for the model and effectively retains its biological representation. The transformations includes normalizers applied sequentially guided by regular expression patterns. The first layer of normalization retains the decimal nature of values that hold numeric information like spatial coordinates and reactivity scores. The second layer preserves integers and standalone units by adding spaces around them, the third layer ensures that underscores are treated as separate tokens which provides clarity when underscores are used in structured tokens like gene CGGBP1. The final 2 layers handle removal of any diacritic characters in the tokens. Experiments

BERT which stands for Bidriectional Encoder Representation from Transformers, is a self-supervised represntation model designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabelled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers Devlin et al. [2019].Although BERT has been proven to be versatile in other applications, it was designed to improve on pre-existing models by using a masked language model (MLM) pre-training objective. This makes it adaptable to various tasks by fine-tuning with additional output layers. The base model used in this project was the bert-base-uncased which is a non case-sensitive model that converts all tokens to lower case before use. BERT learns by masking random tokens in the sequence by replacing them with the [MASK] special token and attempting to predict the correct token correctly during training.

The pipeline implemented in this paper is an MLM fine-tune of BERT to enable it predict values of a given cell’s state and it’s environment with controlled emphasis on the cells spatial context. The models bidirectional learning helps it to learn on a structured sequence, trends for different given positions within the sequence. The vocabulary of the base model was extended to fit the new vocabulary size of the custom tokenizer to prevent unknown-token issues when the model encounters custom tokens. This also allows the custom token transforms to be applied, preventing the model from breaking tokens that should be considered as a whole. A

custom masking strategy was developed to optimize the token masking process within the sequences representing embedded cell states.This approach ensures the model prioritizes learning the variable and contextually significant aspects of the cell state sequence, which are critical for capturing spatial and functional heterogeneity. Custom special tokens like gene and neighbor identifiers that act as fixed reference points across conditions were de-emphasized by reducing the probability of them getting masked during training. Each special token got a masking probability of 5% while tissue type tokens got a probability of 20% and gene names which were not special tokens but fixed vocabulary tokens were given a masking probability of 10%. The masking strategy class had a standard probability of 15% applied to every other token. The tissue type was assigned with the highest masking probability, set at 20% as shown in figure 5, to enhance the models ability to accurately associate specific cell types with their corresponding tissue samples. By increasing tissue type masking priority, the model is hypothesized to develop a more nuanced behavioral pattern identification of similar cell compositions - same HVGs, neighbors, cancer score or other properties, across different TMEs. This approach is particularly beneficial for subsequent unsupervised fine-tuning on TMEs captured from different regions of the body, giving the ability to assess how cells with identical transcriptomes might behave across various organs or what specific conditions within various organs are required to induce and maintain a cell in a particular functional state.
